claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on Strongylocentrotus purpuratus early pluteus larvae at three days post fertilization (dpf).
source: Sea urchin early pluteus larvae were cultured and collected at three dpf. We performed single-cell RNA sequencing on six samples from four independent biological replicates.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the developmental stage and timing of sample collection for scRNA-seq.

claim: Transcriptomes from 19,699 cells were included in the final analysis.
source: In total, transcriptomes from 19,699 cells were included in the final analysis.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of cells analyzed.

claim: Louvain graph clustering revealed 21 genetically distinct cell clusters in the early pluteus larva.
source: To identify sea urchin larval cell types, we used Louvain graph clustering as implemented in the Seurat pipeline (see Materials and methods). This revealed 21 genetically distinct cell clusters (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), each representing an individual cell type or a set of closely related cell types in the early pluteus larva.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the computational method used and the number of clusters identified.

claim: The 21 cell clusters represent cell types from all three embryonic germ layers (endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm).
source: Further, we grouped the cell clusters according to their embryonic germ layer origin (Figure 1C) using knowledge from previous lineage tracing experiments (Angerer and Davidson, 1984; Cameron et al., 1987).
evidence: The manuscript states that cell clusters were grouped by germ layer origin based on previous lineage tracing studies.

claim: A total of 15,578 WHL genes (transcriptome models) and 12,924 genes (SPU gene models) were expressed across all cell types.
source: To validate these identities, we identified all genes expressed in each cell type, totaling in 15,578 WHL genes (transcriptome models) and 12,924 genes (SPU gene models) (Supplementary file 1)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the total number of genes expressed using two different gene model annotations.

claim: Sp-SoxC is expressed in skeletal cells in addition to its previously described expression in early neuronal specification.
source: For instance, the transcription factors Sp-SoxC and Sp-Hbn, previously described in early neuronal specification (Garner et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2016; Yaguchi et al., 2016), were predicted by our scRNA-seq analysis to also be expressed in skeletal cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes novel expression domains for Sp-SoxC based on scRNA-seq data and cites previous studies showing its role in neuronal specification.

claim: Sp-Hbn is expressed in skeletal cells in addition to its previously described expression in early neuronal specification.
source: For instance, the transcription factors Sp-SoxC and Sp-Hbn, previously described in early neuronal specification (Garner et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2016; Yaguchi et al., 2016), were predicted by our scRNA-seq analysis to also be expressed in skeletal cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes novel expression domains for Sp-Hbn based on scRNA-seq data and cites previous studies.

claim: Sp-Fgf9/16/20 is expressed in oral ectoderm, cardiac sphincter, intestine, and anus in addition to its known expression in skeletal cells.
source: Likewise, the FGF signaling ligand, Sp-Fgf9/16/20, is known to be involved in skeletal formation and is expressed in specific populations of PMCs (Adomako-Ankomah and Ettensohn, 2014). ScRNA-seq indicates it is also expressed in oral ectoderm, cardiac sphincter, intestine, and anus (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript describes novel expression domains for Sp-Fgf9/16/20 based on scRNA-seq data and cites previous work on its skeletal expression.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing has higher sensitivity than in situ hybridization for detecting gene expression in coelomic pouch cells.
source: Interestingly, plotting the Juliano and co-authors' gene list, alongside previously described coelomic pouch specific genes (Luo and Su, 2012; Martik and McClay, 2015), they were all found in our analysis to be expressed in the same cell cluster (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). This suggests a higher sensitivity of single-cell RNA sequencing compared to the in situ hybridization, adding crucial missing information on the molecular fingerprint of a complex cell type.
evidence: The manuscript compares detection of genes by scRNA-seq versus in situ hybridization and concludes scRNA-seq is more sensitive.

claim: Cell proliferation markers including pcna, DNA polymerases, DNA ligases, condensins, and centromere proteins are enriched in ciliary band, apical plate, coelomic pouch, immune, and skeletal cell clusters.
source: The majority of cell proliferation genes were found to be enriched in the ciliary band, apical plate, coelomic pouch, immune, and skeletal cell clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which cell clusters show enrichment of proliferation markers.

claim: EdU pulse labeling confirmed S-phase cells in ciliary band, apical plate, oral ectoderm, endodermal and skeletal cells.
source: Validating this, we observed S-phase cells in ciliary band, apical plate, oral ectoderm, endodermal and skeletal cells using Edu pulse labeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental validation of proliferating cells using EdU labeling.

claim: Cell populations derived from the same germ layer share more transcription factors with each other than with cell populations from other germ layers.
source: In general, cell populations derived from the same germ layer shared more factors with each other than with cell populations from other germ layers (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the finding that cell type expression programs often retain information about their developmental lineage (Sladitschek et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this pattern of transcription factor sharing and cites a reference supporting the concept of lineage information retention.

claim: Nearly one third (n = 187) of transcription factors are shared by cell type families from all three germ layers.
source: Further analysis, however, revealed very few transcription factors specific to cells from a single germ layer, contrasting with many regulators expressed in derivatives of more than one germ layer (Figure 3A), and nearly one third (n = 187) shared by cell type families from all three layers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the number of transcription factors shared across all three germ layers.

claim: Mesodermal cell populations share more transcription factors with ectodermal than with endodermal cell populations.
source: Unexpectedly, mesodermal cell populations share expression of more transcription factors with ectodermal than with endodermal cell populations, even though they are more closely linked to endodermal lineage in development.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this unexpected finding about transcription factor sharing patterns.

claim: Cell type families derived from the same germ layer share up to one third of transcription factors, while the majority are cell type-specific.
source: We also noted that cell type families derived from the same germ layer share up to one third of transcription factors, while the majority are cell type-specific (Figure 3B, D and E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the proportion of shared versus specific transcription factors within germ layers.

claim: Most homeobox class transcription factors are enriched in ectodermally derived cell populations in the early pluteus larva.
source: In the early pluteus larva, most homeobox class transcription factors are enriched in ectodermally derived cell populations, such as the apical plate and neurons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the enrichment pattern of homeobox transcription factors.

claim: ANTP Class and HNF class transcription factors are enriched in endodermal derivatives.
source: In contrast, ANTP Class and HNF class transcription factors are enriched in endodermal derivatives (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the enrichment pattern of ANTP and HNF class transcription factors.

claim: Genes involved in specifying coelomic pouch cells are co-expressed in both coelomic pouch and apical plate cells.
source: For instance, we plotted all transcription factors known to be active in specifying coelomic pouch cells (Martik and McClay, 2015). Our data confirmed their co-expression in coelomic pouch, but also revealed their co-expression in the apical plate (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the expression pattern of coelomic pouch specification genes and cites the relevant previous study.

claim: Genes involved in the aboral ectoderm gene regulatory network are expressed in both aboral ectoderm and apical plate cells.
source: Similarly, plotting genes involved in the aboral ectoderm gene regulatory network (Ben-Tabou de-Leon et al., 2013), we found all genes in both the aboral ectoderm cluster as well as in the apical plate cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the expression pattern of aboral ectoderm GRN genes and cites the relevant previous study.

claim: Most members of the pre-gastrula skeletogenic mesoderm regulatory network are still active in the pluteus larva and specific to skeletal cells.
source: On the other hand, plotting members of the pre-gastrula skeletogenic mesoderm regulatory network (Figure 5C) revealed most were still active in the pluteus larva and specific to skeletal cells (Oliveri et al., 2008; Shashikant and Ettensohn, 2019; Khor et al., 2019; Ettensohn, 2020).
evidence: The manuscript describes the expression pattern of skeletogenic GRN genes and cites multiple relevant previous studies.

claim: Subclustering of neuronal cells revealed 12 distinct neuronal populations.
source: In order to investigate this, we independently performed subclustering and re-analysis of the neuronal, immune, and PMC cells. Subclustering of each of these initial major clusters revealed 12 neuronal, 8 immune, and 5 PMC subclusters, each likely representing distinct cell types (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of neuronal subclusters identified through subclustering analysis.

claim: Subclustering of immune cells revealed 8 distinct immune cell populations.
source: Subclustering of each of these initial major clusters revealed 12 neuronal, 8 immune, and 5 PMC subclusters, each likely representing distinct cell types (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of immune cell subclusters identified.

claim: Subclustering of PMC cells revealed 5 distinct PMC populations.
source: Subclustering of each of these initial major clusters revealed 12 neuronal, 8 immune, and 5 PMC subclusters, each likely representing distinct cell types (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of PMC subclusters identified.

claim: Two immune subclusters express polyketide synthase 1 (Sp-Pks1), suggesting they represent sea urchin pigment cell populations.
source: Two of the immune subclusters expressed polyketide synthase 1 (Sp-Pks1), suggesting these represent sea urchin pigment cell populations (Calestani and Rogers, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript identifies pigment cells based on Sp-Pks1 expression and cites a relevant previous study.

claim: A subcluster of immune cells expresses the membrane attack complex/perforin family gene (Sp-MacpfA2), suggesting it corresponds to immune system globular cells.
source: We also found a subcluster of immune cells that expresses the membrane attack complex/perforin family gene (Sp-MacpfA2), suggesting this corresponds to immune system globular cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript identifies globular cells based on Sp-MacpfA2 expression.

claim: The finding of 5 PMC subclusters corroborates previous reports showing five distinct groups of PMC cells along the syncytium.
source: Notably, our finding of 5 PMC subclusters corroborates previous reports showing five distinct groups of PMC cells along the syncytium (Sun and Ettensohn, 2014; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript compares its findings to previous reports and cites the relevant study.

claim: Three neuronal subclusters located in the apical domain express Tryptophan hydroxylase (Tph), suggesting they represent serotonergic neurons.
source: In total, we identified three neuronal subclusters located in the apical domain (subclusters 2, 3 and 4) of the larva that express Tryptophan hydroxylase (Tph), which encodes a key enzyme in the serotonin biosynthesis pathway, suggesting these represent serotonergic neurons in the larva.
evidence: The manuscript identifies serotonergic neurons based on Tph expression and its known role in serotonin biosynthesis.

claim: Two distinct cholinergic neuronal subclusters (7 and 8) were identified within the ciliary band expressing the enzyme involved in acetylcholine biosynthesis (Sp-Chat).
source: Within the ciliary band, which comprises the larva's peripheral nervous system (Slota et al., 2020), we identified two distinct cholinergic subclusters (7 and 8) expressing the enzyme involved in acetylcholine biosynthesis (Sp-Chat) (Figure 6C)
evidence: The manuscript identifies cholinergic neurons based on Sp-Chat expression and cites a reference about the ciliary band.

claim: A neuronal subcluster (9) corresponding to lateral and post-oral neurons co-expresses Sp-Pdx1, Sp-Brn1/2/4, and the neuropeptide Sp-An.
source: Moreover, we identified a neuronal subcluster in close proximity with the ciliary band, which corresponds to the lateral and post-oral neurons (subcluster 9). This population has been previously characterized by our group and was found to co-express Sp-Pdx1, Sp-Brn1/2/4, and the neuropeptide Sp-An (Perillo et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript identifies this neuronal population and cites previous work characterizing it.

claim: Two distinct mouth neuron subtypes (subclusters 10 and 11) were identified based on expression of Sp-Nkx3.2, Sp-Isl, Sp-Salmfap, and tyrosine hydroxylase (Sp-Th).
source: Using gene markers that mark differentiated neurons expressed in the rim of the larva's mouth, including Sp-Nkx3.2 (Wei et al., 2011), Sp-Isl (Perillo et al., 2018), the neuropeptide Sp-Salmfap (Wood et al., 2018), and the enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase (Sp-Th) involved in the dopaminergic pathway, we identified two distinct mouth neurons subtypes (subclusters 10 and 11; Figure 6C).
evidence: The manuscript identifies mouth neuron subtypes based on specific markers and cites relevant previous studies.

claim: A neuronal population (subcluster 12) corresponding to neurons associated with the cardiac sphincter was identified based on co-expression of Sp-Fgfr1 and Sp-Fgf9/16/20.
source: Lastly, we found one neuronal population that, based on its molecular signature, and in particular the co-presence of Sp-Fgfr1 and Sp-Fgf9/16/20 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), could correspond to neurons associated with the cardiac sphincter within the esophageal endoderm (subcluster 12).
evidence: The manuscript identifies this neuronal population based on specific marker expression.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 positive neurons lie in close proximity to the ciliary band and project axons toward both the apical plate and ciliary band.
source: Double immunohistochemical staining of the neuronal marker 1E11 and Sp-An shows that these neurons lie in close proximity to the ciliary band, and project axons toward both the apical plate and ciliary band (Figure 7A1-A3).
evidence: The manuscript describes the anatomical location and projections of these neurons based on immunohistochemistry.

claim: A total of 20 genes involved in the formation and proper function of vertebrate endocrine pancreas are differentially enriched in the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons.
source: We identified a total of 20 genes, all involved in the formation and proper function of vertebrate endocrine pancreas, which are differentially enriched in the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the number of pancreatic-related genes expressed in these neurons.

claim: 249 genes belonging to the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neuron subcluster were differentially expressed in the Pdx1 knockdown dataset, with 65% of the targets being downregulated.
source: In total, we found 249 genes belonging to the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neuron subcluster (9) that were differentially expressed in the Pdx1 knockdown dataset, with 65 % of the targets being downregulated (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly quantifies the number and proportion of differentially expressed genes in Pdx1 knockdown.

claim: Downregulated genes in Pdx1 knockdown include key transcription factors involved in neuronal differentiation (Sp-Brn1/2/4 and Sp-Otp) and terminal differentiation genes (Sp-An, Sp-Ngfffap, Sp-Th, and Sp-Chat).
source: Among the downregulated genes, we found key transcription factors involved in neuronal differentiation, including Sp-Brn1/2/4 and Sp-Otp, as well as terminal differentiation genes important in neuronal signaling, such as Sp-An, Sp-Ngfffap, Sp-Th, and Sp-Chat (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the downregulated genes in Pdx1 knockdown experiments.

claim: Sp-Pdx1 is necessary for the acquisition of the neuronal identity of Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 positive cells.
source: Using differential expression results from Pdx-1 knockdown experiments, we show that Pdx1 is necessary for the acquisition of the neuronal identity of these cells.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on knockdown experiments.

claim: Knockdown of Sp-Pdx1 results in severe downregulation of the Sp-An neuropeptide, compromising the neuroendocrine fate of this neuronal type.
source: As previously described by our group, knockdown of the pancreatic transcription factor Sp-Pdx1 results in severe downregulation of the Sp-An neuropeptide, compromising the neuroendocrine fate of this neuronal type (Perillo et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript describes the effect of Pdx1 knockdown and cites previous work from the same group.

claim: The vertebrate orthologue of Sp-Pdx1 is essential for pancreas development, β-cell differentiation, and maintaining mature β-cell function.
source: The vertebrate orthologue of Sp-Pdx1 is essential for pancreas development, β-cell differentiation, and maintaining mature β-cell function (Kaneto et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript states this fact about the vertebrate Pdx1 orthologue and cites a relevant reference.

claim: Sp-Notch, Sp-Pax6, Sp-Hb9, Sp-Hes, Sp-Ac/Sc, Sp-Mafs and Sp-Gbx2 are all expressed in the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons.
source: From our scRNA-seq analysis, it is evident that Sp-Notch, Sp-Pax6, Sp-Hb9, Sp-Hes, Sp-Ac/Sc (the orthologue of ASCL1), Sp-Mafs and the recently re-annotated Sp-Gbx2 (previously annotated as Sp-Nk7- https://new.echinobase.org) are all expressed in the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists genes expressed in these neurons based on scRNA-seq data.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express the neural cell adhesion molecule Ncam ortholog, which is produced in the nervous system and endocrine cells of the rat.
source: For instance, the ortholog of the neural cell adhesion molecule Ncam known to be produced in the nervous system and endocrine cells of the rat is also expressed in this cluster (Langley et al., 1987).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Ncam expression in these neurons and cites a reference about its expression in rat.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express genes encoding members of the glutamate signaling pathway (Sp-Glt, Sp-Vglut1, Sp-Glur1).
source: Moreover, these neurons also express genes encoding members of the glutamate signaling pathway (Sp-Glt: glutamate synthase; Sp-Vglut1: glutamate transporter; Sp-Glur1: glutamate receptor), which in mammals are involved in glucose-responsive insulin secretion (Gonoi et al., 1994; Maechler and Wollheim, 1999)
evidence: The manuscript identifies glutamate pathway genes in these neurons and cites references about their role in insulin secretion.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express tyrosine hydroxylase (Th), the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine biosynthesis, which is present in the endocrine pancreas of multiple species.
source: Moreover, these neurons also express genes encoding members of the glutamate signaling pathway (Sp-Glt: glutamate synthase; Sp-Vglut1: glutamate transporter; Sp-Glur1: glutamate receptor), which in mammals are involved in glucose-responsive insulin secretion (Gonoi et al., 1994; Maechler and Wollheim, 1999), and tyrosine hydroxylase (Th), the rate-limiting enzyme of catecholamine biosynthesis, which is present in the endocrine pancreas of multiple species (Teitelman et al., 1993; Iturriza and Thibault, 1993).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Th expression in these neurons and cites references about its presence in pancreas.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express choline acetyltransferase (Chat), which is highly expressed in human pancreatic islets and may be essential for stimulation of insulin secretion.
source: Furthermore, Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express choline acetyltransferase (Chat), which has been found to be highly expressed in human pancreatic islets and may be essential for the stimulation of insulin secretion by the neighboring β-cells (Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript identifies Chat expression in these neurons and cites a reference about its role in pancreatic islets.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express the serotonin receptor Sp-5ht7.
source: Transcripts of the sea urchin serotonin receptor Sp-5ht7 are present in Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neuronal population suggesting that serotonin might regulate the neurotransmitter/neuropeptide secretion in a similar way as for insulin.
evidence: The manuscript identifies Sp-5ht7 expression in these neurons.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons express Thyroid hormone receptor B.
source: Similarly, transcripts of the Thyroid hormone receptor B are also found in this population, suggesting that thyroid hormone signaling may play a role to its differentiation similar to the one in murine endocrine pancreas differentiation (Aiello et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript identifies thyroid hormone receptor B expression in these neurons and cites a reference about its role in pancreas.

claim: The Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons produce transcripts of three glucose co-transporter genes (Sp-Slc2a1, Sp-Slc5a9 and Sp-Slc5a9L).
source: Our analysis revealed that the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neurons produce transcripts of three glucose co-transporter genes (Sp-Slc2a1, Sp-Slc5a9 and Sp-Slc5a9L) proposing that they are able to detect such changes in glucose levels similarly to the endocrine pancreas cells.
evidence: The manuscript identifies glucose transporter gene expression in these neurons.

claim: An ancestral neuron in early deuterostomes may have given rise to the endocrine cells in the vertebrate pancreas.
source: Our results confirm and extend this pancreatic-like signature, suggesting that an ancestral neuron in early deuterostomes may have given rise to the endocrine cells in the vertebrate pancreas.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes this evolutionary hypothesis based on the shared molecular features.

claim: A network similar to the one orchestrated by Pdx1 in the sea urchin neurons was active in an ancestral cell type and then inherited by neuronal and pancreatic developmental lineages in sea urchins and vertebrates.
source: We hypothesize that a network similar to the one orchestrated by Pdx1 in the sea urchin neurons was active in an ancestral cell type and then inherited by neuronal and pancreatic developmental lineages in sea urchins and vertebrates.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Echinoderms are a member of the phylogenetic sister group to chordates within deuterostomes.
source: Within deuterostomes, echinoderms are a member of the phylogenetic sister group to chordates, making them an ideal model for understanding the origin and diversification of deuterostome and chordate cell types (Arnone et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript states this phylogenetic relationship and cites a reference.

claim: Sea urchin embryos and larvae are optically transparent, allowing easy observation of different cell types and biological processes.
source: The main reason for this lies in the ease with which different cell types and biological processes can be observed in the optically transparent embryos and larvae.
evidence: The manuscript states this characteristic of sea urchin embryos and larvae.

claim: The 10x Genomics Chromium scRNA-seq system was used for single-cell RNA sequencing.
source: Individual samples were dissociated into single cells using a gentle enzyme-free dissociation protocol and using the 10 x Chromium scRNA-seq system (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the technology platform used.

claim: Of the 29,130 cells estimated by Cell Ranger, 19,699 cells passed the quality checks and were further analyzed.
source: Of the 29,130 cells estimated by Cell Ranger, 19,699 cells passed the quality checks and were further analyzed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of cells before and after quality control.

claim: The proportion of pancreatic genes expressed in the Sp-Pdx1/Sp-Brn1/2/4 neuronal subcluster in actual data is significantly different from randomized data (p-value < 0.002).
source: Then, we have performed a chi-squared test within R (Hope, 1968) to show that the proportion from the actual data proportion is significantly different to the randomized data proportion with p-value less than 0.002.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the statistical test result comparing actual versus randomized data.

claim: The sea urchin larva consists of 21 genetically distinct cell clusters representing distinct cell type families.
source: Our findings suggest that the larva consists of 21 genetically distinct cell clusters, representing distinct cell type families (Shekhar and Menon, 2019), which we validate using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) and immunohistochemistry (IHC).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding and mentions validation methods.

claim: Most transcription factors are expressed pleiotropically independently of their germ layer origins, yet tend to be cell type family-specific within a germ layer.
source: Comparing the transcription factor content of the grouped cell clusters reveals that most transcription factors are expressed pleiotropically independently of their germ layer origins, yet tend to be cell type family-specific within a germ layer.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this pattern of transcription factor expression.

claim: The study identified 12 distinct neuronal cell types in the sea urchin larva.
source: Lastly, we investigate neuronal diversity in the sea urchin larva, identifying 12 distinct neuronal cell types.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of neuronal cell types identified.

claim: Sp-Pdx1 has an evolutionary conserved role as a mediator of endocrine fate.
source: Supporting this, knockdown of Sp-Pdx1 shows it is necessary for differentiation of this pancreatic-like neuronal endocrine population, indicating it has an evolutionary conserved role as a mediator of endocrine fate.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on knockdown experiments.

claim: The study used an enzyme-free dissociation protocol to dissociate larvae into single cells.
source: Individual samples were dissociated into single cells using a gentle enzyme-free dissociation protocol and using the 10 x Chromium scRNA-seq system (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the dissociation method used.

claim: Cell viability was assessed using Propidium Iodide and Fluorescein diacetate, and only specimens with cell viability ≥ 90% were further processed.
source: Cell viability was assessed via using Propidium Iodide and Fluorescein diacetate and only specimens with cell viability ≥ 90 % were further processed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the viability assessment method and threshold.

claim: Libraries were sequenced for 75 bp paired-end reads on an Illumina NextSeq 500, resulting in a mean of 88 M reads.
source: Libraries were sequenced by GeneCore (EMBL, Heidelberg, Germany) for 75 bp paired-end reads (Illumina NextSeq 500), resulting in a mean of 88 M reads.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sequencing parameters and output.

claim: The Strongylocentrotus purpuratus genome version 3.1 was used for alignment of single-cell RNA-seq reads.
source: The genomic index was made in Cell Ranger using the S. purpuratus genome version 3.1 (Sea Urchin Genome Sequencing Consortium et al., 2006; Kudtarkar and Cameron, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the genome version used and cites relevant references.

claim: Genes transcribed in less than three cells and cells with less than 200 transcribed genes were excluded from the analysis.
source: Genes that are transcribed in less than three cells and cells that have less than a minimum of 200 transcribed genes were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the filtering criteria used.

claim: The study used Seurat v3.0.2 R package for single-cell RNA-seq analysis.
source: Cell Ranger output matrices for four biological and two technical replicates were used for further analysis in Seurat v3.0.2 R package (Stuart et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the software package and version used, with citation.
